Football fans and players in Argentina are mourning the death of teenage footballer Abel Nunez, who died after su
items.text:
Argentina mourns teen footballer Nunez who died after on-pitch collision
Abel Nunez, 16, died after suffering a severe blow to the head during a youth football match for his club Ezeiza.
Football fans and players in Argentina are mourning the death of teenage footballer Abel Nunez, who died after suffering a head injury during a youth match last week.
Nunez suffered a severe blow to the head during a fifth division youth match between his club FC Ezeiza and Muniz on Friday and died two days later, according to reports in Argentinian media.
Shortly after the on-field incident, the 16-year-old’s club posted a statement saying he suffered a “severe head injury that required surgery” and called on supporters to participate in a prayer chain.
Following his death, Argentine social media was flooded with an outpouring of shock and messages of condolence for Nunez’s family and friends, said Argentinian news outlet TN Deportivo.
“With profound sorrow and immense sadness, we say goodbye to a young man who had his whole life ahead of him and who today leaves us with a void impossible to describe,” his club said.
“After suffering a hard blow during a match, proudly wearing our Ezeiza shirt, we deeply regret his departure.
“Today football is in the background. We are overwhelmed by the pain of saying goodbye to a colleague, a young man full of dreams and hopes, who was part of our family.
“May you rest in peace. You will always be part of our family.”
Born in 2008, Nunez was a native of Ezeiza, a city within the Greater Buenos Aires region. He played both football and futsal regularly, according to the information he shared on his Facebook profile.
Nunez’s futsal team, Nueva Estrella, also joined in the mourning and announced a suspension of activities.
“You will always be with us. Your memory will live forever in our hearts,” the club wrote on social media.
Roman Corral, the father of the teenager’s best friend, gave a heartbreaking account of how the young man’s teammates and loved ones are coping with their grief.
“The boys are devastated; it’s something unnatural for them. At that age, you think you’re a superhero, and to lose your life like that, the way Abel lost his… I’ve known him since he was 12, when he started school with my son in first grade. His dream was to be a football player, just like my son,” Corral told Radio La Red in Argentina.
Corral used the radio programme to send a direct message to the Argentine football authorities: “If anyone from the AFA is listening, please observe a minute of silence. He wanted to live as a footballer and he should be given a send-off as a footballer because he died on the pitch, doing what all Argentinians love, which is playing football.”

items.title: Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president
items.summary:
Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president
- Published
A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight
items.text:
Florida pastor found guilty over role in assassination of Haitian president
- Published
A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight charges against him, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison.
The 67-year-old was accused of being involved in a plot to replace Moïse as Haiti's president with himself in 2021, allegedly so he could award lucrative contracts to a Florida-based security outfit once in place.
The murder of Moïse has left Haiti without a leader for five years. That political vacuum has intensified gang violence in the impoverished Caribbean nation.
A presidential election is scheduled for next year and Moïse's wife, Martine, who was injured in the attack that killed her husband, announced this week that she intended to stand.
Sanon was found guilty on Wednesday following an eight-week trial in federal court in Miami, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that he intends to appeal against the verdict, it reports.
Prosecutors said Sanon had "political aspirations" in Haiti and, in April 2021, met several other co-conspirators to devise a plan to oust Moïse in an armed raid on the presidential palace in the capital, Port-au-Prince.
Among them were the heads of the companies Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security - collectively referred to as CTU - who would finance the coup in exchange for government contracts for infrastructure projects, and to provide security forces and equipment.
A few months later, the other conspirators realised that Sanon had "neither the constitutional qualifications nor the popular support" to become Haiti's president and so shifted to another candidate, the US Department of Justice said.
At the same time, the plot had developed from one to forcibly remove Moïse from office to assassinating him, investigators said.
Dozens of people have been implicated in the conspiracy, which prosecutors said involved co-ordinating funding for and delivering weapons and mercenaries to Haiti to carry out the attack.
On 6 July that year, a group of Colombian mercenaries entered the presidential palace and killed Moïse. His wife, who was also injured in the attack, said at the time that the assailants had "riddled" her husband with bullets.
The successful assassination plot raised questions in Haiti about the relative ease with which the mercenaries were able to gain access to the president.
The country - the poorest in the Americas - has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but Moïse's assassination ushered in a period of worsening instability that emboldened gangs and prompted the deployment of a multinational force.
However, this has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway and more than 5,700 people have been killed or injured in the year to 11 September, the UN said last month.
Sanon and several other co-conspirators were arrested by Haitian authorities, while three mercenaries were killed in a gun battle with police. Eighteen people were transferred to Florida in September to stand trial over the plot.
Four men, including the heads of the CTU, were convicted of their role earlier this year. Sanon had been scheduled to be tried with them, but his case was delayed due to health reasons, according to CBS.
Sanon was born in Haiti but moved to the US as a teenager. He told the court he had worked in churches in Haitian immigrant communities in several parts of the US including Florida, US media report.

items.summary:
Myanmar committed genocide against Muslim Rohingya minority, UN court finds
The United Nations International Court of Justice on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority. It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court.
The
items.text:
Myanmar committed genocide against Muslim Rohingya minority, UN court finds
The United Nations International Court of Justice on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority. It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court.
The top United Nations court ruled on Thursday that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces against the Rohingya Muslim minority population in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.
The decision, seven years after the case was filed by predominantly Muslim Gambia, marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the legal threshold to prove genocide had been met. It was the first time the court held a state responsible for genocide.
"The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya," presiding Judge Yuji Iwasawa said in a reading of the decision.
Read more'Targeted for destruction': Top UN court hears Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
The panel found "that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in Northern Rakhine State".
Judges found that Myanmar's military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations. The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said.
Myanmar's military offensive drove at least 700,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
A panel of 15 judges said "the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group namely the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine state", meeting the legal threshold for genocide.
The court's ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
'Justice'
For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world's largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the historic ruling offers a glimmer of hope for accountability.
"I want justice," a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor said in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family.
"There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this," she said, requesting anonymity.
Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and cruelty towards families and children.
Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, the panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar's actions constitute genocide.
The case was brought by the Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II.
While the ICJ has no way of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.
He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.
This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.
Myanmar has always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.
"Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein," its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January.
'Targeted for destruction'
The Gambia's justice minister said the country filed the case "after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years".
The Gambia has the "full backing and support" of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow.
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," added Jallow.
"The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction."
Genocide is notoriously difficult to prove in international law because the Convention requires proof of a specific "intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group".
The Gambia argued during the hearings that genocidal intent was clear from the "organised nature and execution" of the crackdown, its "extreme brutality", the "pervasive sexual violence", and the targeting of children.
Legal experts are watching the case closely for clues as to how the ICJ will handle another seminal case before it – accusations by South Africa that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the verdict would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military.
"They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead," Osman, 20, told AFP.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

items.title: Washington Spirit v Kansas City Current: where the NWSL Championship will be won and lost
items.summary: This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current p
items.text:
This year’s NWSL Championship blends recurring themes with some newness. For the familiar: the Washington Spirit are in the final for the third straight year, hoping the third time’s the charm after back-to-back 1-0 defeats in their past two attempts. Slightly familiar, too, is Kansas City Current playing the championship game at Washington’s Audi Field, where they lost the final to Portland in 2022 and where they will contend again Saturday.
For the novelty? Neither Kansas City nor Washington, despite their modern dominance in the NWSL table, have won the championship since 2021 (when Washington won). With Gotham’s bid for a two-peat stymied by the Current in the semi-final, here are five things that will decide a new winner in 2026.
Washington’s defensive pressure Washington have allowed the second-fewest goals in the NWSL this year. Through the season and into the playoffs, the center-back pairing of the English defender Esme Morgan and Tara Rudd, the Scottish goalkeeper Sandy MacIver (fourth-highest save percentage in NWSL) and the defensive midfielder Andi Sullivan have been tough to break through for even the league’s most elite attackers. Further up the field, the Spirit’s defense begins with an attacking unit fond of forcing mistakes that lead to goals, with the late-season addition of Clara Luvanga (who has seven goal contributions in seven games for the Spirit) a key impact.
Kansas City, who have scored more goals than any other NWSL team this year, will be a challenge. Defending set pieces will be a space to watch, as they provided the only goal Utah scored against the Spirit in the semi-final, and all the goals Kansas City scored against Gotham.
Bethune on a mission against former team This season’s Midfielder of the Year is representing a team in the NWSL Championship for the third straight year (her second with availability to play). But this will be her first not representing the Spirit. After leaving Washington for Missouri in February, Bethune is facing her former team for the chance to win her first championship trophy.
A bit more poetry: Bethune nearly broke the NWSL’s all-time single-season assists record during her 2024 rookie season for the Spirit. (A torn meniscus cut short her streak, but she still was named Rookie of the Year.) She finally broke it this season with Kansas City. Her creative influence in the Current’s midfield has been crucial to unlocking their goal-scoring capabilities. Bethune’s ability to pull apart Washington’s laudable defensive structure could prove crucial in the final.
Kansas City’s attacking depth Temwa Chawinga is a two-time NWSL MVP for a reason, but she wasn’t the sole source of Kansas City’s 54 goals in 30 regular season games. The Current’s past nine goals (across five games including the playoffs) were scored by six different players, with Haley Hopkins (tied with Chawinga for goal contributions in the regular season) notching four of them. Chawinga enters the Championship with only one goal contribution in five games and no goals since 3 October, but she can break through at any moment. If not, the Current’s surrounding cast of contributors – Hopkins, Michelle Cooper, Bethune and Debinha – seems prepared to make the difference.
Rodman is the Spirit’s gamechanger The Spirit also have attacking depth, but Rodman is a gamechanger whose impact is more lopsided. Her 20 goal contributions in the regular season were more than double the goal contributions of any teammate, and that’s without quantifying the space she frees up for fellow goalscorers with her calculated off-the-ball movements.
In the postseason, Rodman has four goal contributions in two games – two goals and two assists. Coming at the end of one of her best club seasons, a big performance in the final will be essential for a Spirit victory. It would also further solidify her as one of the deserved main characters (and highest-paid player) in the NWSL.
Will Rowdy Audi make a difference? Stadium squabbles were an unexpected storyline of this year’s postseason. Gotham and Washington faced scheduling hurdles that called into question their home-field advantage and/or forced them to play on less-than-ideal pitches for their semi-finals. But this Saturday, the Spirit will still have home-field advantage at Audi Field, where they’ve earned the trust of a robust home crowd. Whether Washington can turn that familiar, friendly space into the perfect scene for actually lifting the trophy in their third straight final would be a poetic end to the postseason’s stadium woes.

items.summary:
ICJ: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
November 19, 2026
The International Court of Justice on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 1
items.text:
ICJ: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
November 19, 2026
The International Court of Justice on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and if necessary prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
What is the case about?
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predomiantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.
The Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
What else did Judge Iwasawa say as he read out the verdict?
The ICJ said that by its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But he also said that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and if anything fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
This is a developing story, more to follow...

United States President Donald Trump has accused Iran of exploring chemical and biological weapons, reigniting allegations that Tehran may be planning a “dirty bomb” attack.
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Trump said Iran was “look
items.text:
Trump claims Iran is developing bioweapons: Is there any evidence?
United States President Donald Trump has accused Iran of exploring chemical and biological weapons, reigniting allegations that Tehran may be planning a “dirty bomb” attack.
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Trump said Iran was “looking at gases, looking at bio”, without providing evidence to support his claims.
Trump claimed Tehran has pivoted away from developing nuclear capabilities given that “we’ve shut them out”. “We’ll see what happens after January 1,” he said, before referring to Iranians as “nasty people”.
His comments follow a report by CNN on Tuesday citing US intelligence indicating that Iran may be developing plans to target senior officials in Trump’s administration with a chemical weapon in Washington, DC.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed concerns about a possible Iranian attack, saying the US does not face an “imminent threat”. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Rubio’s conclusion, confirming there was no indication of an upcoming attack.
But Trump did not dismiss the possibility. Asked whether people in Washington, DC, should be concerned about a potential attack, Trump said he did not believe so, but threatened retaliation if it happened.
“If it does happen, we wipe them out,” he said.
Is there evidence that Iran possesses a ‘dirty bomb’?
Iran is a signatory to the Biological Weapons Convention, but it ratified it six years before the 1979 revolution that overthrew the Pahlavi monarchy and established the Islamic Republic of Iran. It is also a party to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), ratified in 1997.
Nonetheless, Western intelligence agencies have long maintained that Iran is pursuing unconventional capabilities.
According to a report by a British think tank, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), Iran’s biological weapons programme is believed to have accelerated since the Iran-Iraq War, which ended in 1988.
After Iraq extensively used chemical weapons during that conflict, Tehran resolved never again to accept such an asymmetry in unconventional capabilities, RUSI concluded. What followed was a sustained effort to develop biological agents under the cover of civilian research.
Hamish de Bretton-Gordon, an analyst and former British Army officer, said it would not be surprising if Iran was resorting to developing chemical weapons after US military strikes on its nuclear facilities set back its nuclear programme.
“It is also possible they are looking at biological weapons,” de Bretton-Gordon told Al Jazeera. “With the advent of AI-enabled bio weapons, they have the potential to be as devastating as nuclear weapons at a fraction of the cost and time.”
Such weapons could “replace their nuclear programme [and] be far more difficult to detect”, he added.
According to Dan Kaszeta, an associate fellow at RUSI focussing on defence against chemical, biological and radiological weapons, “this is an area where things are incredibly vague”.
“Any country with the industry, science and laboratory infrastructure that Iran has could, in theory, make chemical and biological hazards in sufficient quantity for a singular incident like a localised terrorist attack,” Kaszeta told Al Jazeera. “The underlying technology is not highly sophisticated.”
“As far as whether Iran has had a chemical or biological weapons programme has been debated for decades, ever since the Iran-Iraq war,” he added. “There have been arguments put forward on both sides of that hypothesis, without any firm conclusion.”
Jacek Siewiera, nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center, separated scientific expertise operational weapons capability from the political willingness to conduct an attack.
“A research programme does not, by itself, establish the ability to carry out a particular operation abroad,” Siewiera told Al Jazeera. “A credible assessment would require corroborated information about capability, operational reach and intent. I would therefore be cautious about assigning a probability to the specific scenario described.”
Echoing WMD allegations about Iraq
This is not the first time the US has accused an enemy of possessing unconventional weapons.
Glen Rangwala, associate professor in the Department of Politics and International Studies at the University of Cambridge, in the UK, said: “There is a fairly extensive history of successive US administrations making unfounded allegations about countries of the Middle East possessing weapons of mass destruction (WMD).”
“It serves to raise the stakes internationally and put potential domestic critics on the back foot,” Rangwala told Al Jazeera.
Washington launched an invasion of Iraq in 2003 after claiming that Saddam Hussein’s government posed an imminent threat due to its alleged chemical, biological and nuclear programmes.
A Senate committee found the CIA and others in George W Bush’s administration manipulated evidence to justify the occupation of Iraq, calling the operation a “whitewash for the White House.”
No stockpiles of banned weapons, nor evidence of a programme to develop any, were ever found in Iraq following the US-led military action.
Rangwala said this tendency to level accusations against rivals has been matched by “an extensive history of successive US administrations not acknowledging how some of its allies in the Middle East have or host WMD”.
“There are good reasons to be concerned about proliferation, but not only on one side of the balance,” he added.

items.title: Maraga-led opposition coalition proposes sweeping changes to Elections Act
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Former Chief Justice David Maraga has led opposition leaders in proposing sweeping amendments to the Elections Act ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Maraga, who convened the People’s Coalition on Election Reforms in Nairobi alongside Democratic Party leader JB Muturi and Li
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Former Chief Justice David Maraga has led opposition leaders in proposing sweeping amendments to the Elections Act ahead of the 2027 General Election.
Maraga, who convened the People’s Coalition on Election Reforms in Nairobi alongside Democratic Party leader JB Muturi and Linda Mwananchi Movement’s Caroli Omondi, said the proposals seek to strengthen the integrity and transparency of the electoral process.
Among the proposed changes is a comprehensive clean-up of the voters’ register to eliminate duplicate, deceased and ineligible voters while ensuring all qualified Kenyans are registered.
The coalition is also seeking the abolition of the national presidential tallying centre at Bomas of Kenya, proposing that results declared at constituency level be considered final.
“Under the proposal, the national tallying centre would only receive, aggregate and announce results already declared by constituency returning officers,” the opposition leaders said in a statement.
The opposition leaders are further proposing electronic voting for Kenyans living abroad, arguing that the estimated 1.4 million citizens in the diaspora should be able to participate without travelling to Kenyan embassies.
They also want voting, counting and declaration of results at polling stations and tallying centres livestreamed to enhance transparency and public accountability.
Maraga said the coalition would submit its irreducible minimum demands to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).
“We will not rest until the Commission is freed from state capture and Kenyans have a free, fair and credible election,” he said.

items.title: Harmer stars as South Africa beat Bangladesh
items.summary:
South Africa vs Bangladesh: Simon Harmer stars as Proteas seal nine-wicket first Test win
South Africa edged closer to securing a spot in the World Test Championship final with a nine-wicket victory against Bangladesh on Thursday; Simon Harmer took four wickets to bowl out Bangladesh; watch the seco
items.text:
South Africa vs Bangladesh: Simon Harmer stars as Proteas seal nine-wicket first Test win
South Africa edged closer to securing a spot in the World Test Championship final with a nine-wicket victory against Bangladesh on Thursday; Simon Harmer took four wickets to bowl out Bangladesh; watch the second Test live on Sky Sports Cricket
Thursday 19 November 2026 12:19, UK
Simon Harmer ran through Bangladesh's tail and South Africa knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first Test by nine wickets on Thursday, taking a 1-0 lead in the teams' two-match series.
The win sees the Proteas edge closer to securing a spot at the World Test Championship final at The Kia Oval in 2027, with the defending champions having dethroned Australia to go top of the ICC rankings following their series win last month.
Resuming on 100-5 at the Wanderers, Bangladesh's lower-order batters couldn't handle the off-spin of Harmer, who took four of the remaining five wickets to help dismiss the tourists for 168 and return figures of 6-51.
- Cameron Bancroft blows open 'Sandpapergate' with statement
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW
- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
It revived memories of Harmer taking 6-16 on day five of the series-clinching victory over Australia last month.
"I don't think I bowled my best this match," Harmer told SuperSport.
"But I'm very aware of the way cricket works; you're going to have days where you bowl well and don't necessarily get rewards.
"Sometimes you don't bowl as well as you should, but you end up getting wickets.
"It would have been tricky if we were chasing 150 or 170. To be able to restrict them and get wickets in the third innings is enjoyable and it's always nice to contribute."
There is bad news for South Africa, though, who are likely to be without their captain Temba Bavuma for the second Test, live on Sky Sports, with the skipper still struggling to overcome a fitness issue.
The Proteas lost first-innings century-maker Marques Ackerman - for a second-ball duck - on the way to reaching their target before lunch at 12-1. Soon after getting bowled off a no-ball, Aiden Markram (8 not out) scored the winning run.
In Harmer, South Africa have a 37-year-old player enjoying a renaissance in a Test career that was drifting until a year ago, when he returned after a two-and-a-half-year absence. He is now a reliable match-winner.
Having already removed Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mahfijul Islam late on day four, Harmer took the final four wickets of the match in his brilliant four-over burst that came after overnight batter Litton Das got an inside edge and played onto his own stumps off Kagiso Rabada (3-46).
Mushfiqur Rahim added 34 runs to his overnight five before gloving Harmer to a close fielder, for a dismissal that was only given after the Proteas reviewed a not-out call.
In his next over, Harmer had Mehidy Hasan Miraz stumped for four before removing Hasan Mahmud (4) and Ebadot Hossain (0) in consecutive balls to wrap up the innings.
Despite making 400 in the first innings after winning the toss, Bangladesh barely avoided an innings defeat.

items.title: Germany news: Pistorius to visit Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
items.summary:
Germany news: Pistorius to visit Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Defense Minister Oscar Pistorius talks security in Poland
- Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
- UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank
items.text:
Germany news: Pistorius to visit Auschwitz memorial in Poland trip
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Defense Minister Oscar Pistorius talks security in Poland
- Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
- UniCredit and Germany reach Commerzbank takeover agreement
Here is a roundup of the biggest headlines from Germany on Thursday, November 19:
UniCredit and Germany reach agreement on Commerzbank takeover
Italian commercial bank UniCredit and the German government reached agreement on the big sticking points of its takeover of Commerzbank.
The EU greenlit UniCredit's takeover of Germany's Commerzbank earlier this week.
The merging of UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion ($1.4 trillion) in assets
across two of the eurozone's largest economies.
It would be one of the most significant cross-border European banking deals in years.
In a statement to Reuters news agency, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Germany "supports a swift process and an orderly transition of control."
"We have reached common ground and UniCredit has made clear commitments to Germany as a business location, to the rights of
Commerzbank employees and to a continued constructive dialogue with the works council," Klingbeil said, referring to a body of elected employee representatives.
Among the concessions, Germany is said to have given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank.
Meanwhile, UniCredit agreed to the key German demand to keep UniCredit's enlarged German business headquartered and listed in Frankfurt.
UniCredit also reportedly pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.
Defense Minister Oscar Pistorious heads to Poland
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will travel to Poland for a two-day visit.
Pistorius is scheduled to meet his Polish counterpart, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, in the capital Warsaw for talks on defense policy.
Poland is a member of both the EU and NATO and is one of the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
The trip to Germany's neighbor to the east will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Auschwitz-Birkenau is one of the biggest symbols of the Holocaust and Germany's Nazi regime, with some 1.1 million people having died in the camp between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews.
The camp's victims were shot, murdered in gas chambers or died of starvation and disease.
Germany warns of cyber security risks in gadgets
The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) said in a report that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals.
According to the report, the number of hacked systems has nearly doubled within a year, with BSI reporting some 75,400 infected systems in Germany to internet providers every day, an 89% increase. Some of the gadgets were found to be already infected at the factory, the report says.
The vast majority of cases involved Android devices, particularly consumer electronics connected to the so-called "Internet of Things."
BSI said criminals rent the hijacked devices as proxy botnets on the dark web to hide their own attacks, which would allow for consumers themselves to unknowingly come under investigators' scrutiny.
BSI President Claudia Plattner has also warned of AI-driven attacks.
"The disruption coming in particular from high-performance, agentic AI has set new benchmarks," she said.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will head to Poland today to talk security with one the most important political and military allies of Ukraine.
His trip will begin with a stop at the memorial site of the former Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz-Birkenau, which was built during the German occupation of Poland during World War II.
Meanwhile, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security has warned that cheap gadgets such as streaming boxes are increasingly being hijacked by cybercriminals

items.title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
items.summary:
Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., on the Democratic Party's agenda for the new Congress
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
items.text:
Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., on the Democratic Party's agenda for the new Congress
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.
"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.
Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.
The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."
She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.
But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.
Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.
The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.
Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.
"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.

items.title: Denmark parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
items.summary:
Denmark parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
All 109 Danish lawmakers present approved the deal, easing tensions over Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
The Danish parliament has unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland, aimed at
items.text:
Denmark parliament approves security deal with Greenland and US
All 109 Danish lawmakers present approved the deal, easing tensions over Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
The Danish parliament has unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States covering Greenland, aimed at bolstering security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Thursday’s decision to approve the deal signed in September eases tensions over US President Donald Trump’s desire to annex the Arctic island.
In the 179-seat parliament, known as the Folketing, the 109 members present voted in favour of the text, which was adopted without opposition or abstention.
The vote, which followed the second reading of the text, went through without any debate or opposition.
In early November, Greenland’s parliament had passed it by 16 votes, with seven abstentions.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory home to 57,000 people.
The deal is not subject to a vote by the US Senate. The executive agreement, following Thursday’s vote in Copenhagen, will enter into force once the Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.
Signed in New York on September 22, the agreement supplements a 1951 accord on the US military presence in Greenland.
It allows the US to build two military bases in Greenland and blocks countries outside the European Union and NATO from strategic sectors, in order to stop China or Russia from gaining influence over the territory, particularly through investments.
Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark, but the deal is to remain in force even if Greenland gains full independence.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that the US needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and other partners.
The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is located.

items.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
items.summary:
Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
- Published
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday
items.text:
Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
- Published
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
Automatic gunfire could be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
- Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show 
  - Published16 January
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

items.text:
Nations Championship: Dan Sheehan starts at No 8 for Ireland vs South Africa and Sam Prendergast plays after avoiding ban
Ireland hooker and captain Dan Sheehan has been shifted out of position to start at No 8 for the visit of South Africa to Dublin in Saturday's Nations Championship (4.40pm) in unusual and risky Andy Farrell move; Fly-half Sam Prendergast starts after citing against him dismissed
Thursday 19 November 2026 14:08, UK
Andy Farrell has named Dan Sheehan out of position at No 8 for Ireland's crunch Nations Championship Test against South Africa in Dublin on Saturday.
The unusual move, with Sheehan's ordinary position at hooker, comes with Ireland missing trio Caelan Doris, Jack Conan and Sean Jansen due to injury.
Sheehan has only played at No 8 once in his career to date, starting there for Leinster against Munster in last month's URC contest at the Aviva Stadium - a clash in which Leinster badly lost the breakdown battle before coming through to win.
Other changes see full-back Hugo Keenan, centre Robbie Henshaw and lock Joe McCarthy return to the squad to start.
Fly-half Sam Prendergast starts the contest after a citing against him for a hip-drop tackle was dismissed on Wednesday.
Wings Rob Baloucoune and Mack Hansen remain to form the back-three with Keenan, while Stuart McCloskey - who played most of last week's victory over Fiji off the bench - partners Henshaw in midfield.
Scrum-half Jamison Gibson-Park retains his starting place, with Craig Casey staying on the bench.
Into the forwards, Ronan Kelleher starts at hooker with Sheehan at No 8, while props Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong start either side of Kelleher in the front-row.
Tadhg Beirne starts again in the second row, alongside McCarthy, while Ryan Baird starts at blindside flanker and Josh van der Flier at openside ahead of Nick Timoney.
On the bench, replacement tighthead Sam Illo has been passed fit to be involved, while hooker Tom Stewart, loosehead Tom O'Toole, lock James Ryan, fly-half Ciaran Frawley and centre Bundee Aki complete the squad alongside Timoney and Casey.
Ireland squad to face South Africa in Nations Championship
Ireland: 15 Hugo Keenan, 14 Robert Baloucoune, 13 Robbie Henshaw, 12 Stuart McCloskey, 11 Mack Hansen, 10 Sam Prendergast, 9 Jamison Gibson-Park; 1 Andrew Porter, 2 Ronan Kelleher, 3 Tadhg Furlong, 4 Joe McCarthy, 5 Tadhg Beirne, 6 Ryan Baird, 7 Josh van der Flier, 8 Dan Sheehan (c).
Replacements: 16 Tom Stewart, 17 Tom O'Toole, 18 Sam Illo, 19 James Ryan, 20 Nick Timoney, 21 Craig Casey, 22 Ciaran Frawley, 23 Bundee Aki.
Springboks recall Etzebeth for crunch clash with Ireland in Dublin
For South Africa, they have recalled experienced lock Eben Etzebeth for the Nations Championship Test in Dublin, one of five changes to the starting XV that lost to France in Paris.
Etzebeth is set to extend his Springbok record to 148 caps by partnering Ruan Nortje in the second row, with Cameron Hanekom coming in at No 8 as Jasper Wiese serves a four-match suspension after his red card against the French.
Props Ox Nche and Wilco Louw plus hooker Malcolm Marx, who were originally selected as the front row last weekend before being replaced just before kick-off in a tactical switch, have been named in the starting XV again.
The backline remains the same with Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu at fly-half and Morne van den Berg the preferred scrum-half.
South Africa will likely need to beat Ireland to reach the Nations Championship final, although a losing bonus point could be enough if England defeat New Zealand and deny the All Blacks any bonus points.
"This is a massive match for us and we know the magnitude of facing Ireland in Dublin, so we felt it was important to strike a balance between consistency in selection, while managing some players and giving others who have been training hard and putting up their hands a chance in what will be a challenging encounter," coach Rassie Erasmus said.
Erasmus is now serving a six-Test suspension following extraordinary claims, saying "match-fixing" and "manipulation" was occurring in rugby.

items.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
items.summary:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be
items.text:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

items.title: Inside women’s football’s difficult rise in Syria: ‘A joy that everyone in the country needed’
items.summary: In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the
items.text:
In December 2024, Syria’s under-18 women’s football team boarded a last-minute bus at midnight from Aqaba, bound for Damascus. The players had been in Jordan preparing for their final match of the WAFF women’s championship, where a win against Saudi Arabia would have kept their hopes of winning the title alive. Syria pulled out amid fears that the border would close.
Back home, a war that had been largely frozen for four years was suddenly moving at pace. Rebel forces had swept out of the northwest, taking Aleppo and were pushing south towards the capital, 350km away, threatening to topple the now-former president, Bashar al-Assad. Players from the provinces around Damascus made their way home. But those from Hasakah, in the country’s far north-east, spent the next three days stranded at Damascus airport, as airline staff fled and planes sat idle on the tarmac, until a bus was finally able to take them home.
Scared, exhausted and running on adrenaline, the team had lived through another episode of disruption; but in truth they had rarely known stability. For Syrian women’s footballers, navigating uncertainty had been part of the game long before the country’s political upheaval reached its latest turning point. “My generation was burned away and completely lost,” said Noor Jumaa, a former national team goalkeeper. “It was like everything that was being built just disappeared.”
After 14 years of war, Syria has much to rebuild. Women’s football is among the institutions trying to recover from a conflict that erased an entire generation of players, interrupted the development of the game itself and left its infrastructure struggling. Yet, in recent years, Syria’s youth teams have emerged as one of the country’s more unexpected sporting success stories, winning regional titles and producing players who are beginning to make their mark abroad.
Syria’s women’s national team played their first international match in 2005. By 2011, plans were under way for an 11-a-side women’s league. Then the uprising began, and all plans were abandoned. For the next six years, women’s football in Syria effectively stopped. There were no international fixtures at any level, only occasional futsal tournaments. More than six million people eventually fled Syria, including hundreds involved in the sport, leaving an already small pool of players scattered across the world.
Men’s football, by contrast, continued. The national team played matches abroad after Syria was barred from hosting fixtures in 2011 on security grounds. The Assad regime used its successes to project an image of normality, even welcoming the squad to his palace after their 2012 WAFF Championship victory. Fifa, despite its rules against political interference, stayed silent.
Girls growing up in those years had no women’s team to watch. “I was watching a match of Syria’s men’s national team, and I was really upset. I would say, ‘God, if only they’d make a national team for girls,’” recalled Raneem Abo Lateef, a 21-year-old goalkeeper for Syria. The opportunity came unexpectedly after her family moved houses, and a girl next door told Abo Lateef that a relative was starting a girls’ club. “Girls’ football? Wow,” she said. “It was like dreams coming true.”
Similarly, international teammate Julnar Mustafa spent hours playing with boys in her neighbourhood in Hasakah. Born in 2008, so too young to remember the beginning of the uprising, she filmed herself dribbling and performing tricks on her phone, uploading the videos to Facebook. A regional coach came across them and invited Mustafa to join his team.
But finding an opportunity to play was only part of the challenge. “In our society, especially in the north, in Hasakah, sport is completely off-limits for girls,” Mustafa told the Guardian. “Not football, not anything”.
While a new generation of girls were finding their way into football, the national team was attempting to return to international competition. In April 2017, Syria entered the Asian Cup qualifiers in Vietnam, assembling a squad after six years without any activity. The federation announced tryouts on Facebook, and players were given about a month of preparation. Syria went on to lose every match, including a 14-0 defeat by Myanmar. “Honestly, it was one of the worst teams in Syria’s history,” said Jumaa, who was part of that squad. “We lost by terrifying scores.”
Maha Al-Katreb, also in the squad at the time, remembers the criticism that followed. Players were ridiculed despite having had little preparation. At the tournament, she saw opponents arrive with larger coaching staffs and younger players training alongside their senior teams. The gap between Syria and their regional competitors was difficult to ignore.
With injuries ending her career early, Al-Katreb fell into coaching by chance and turned towards building a programme that could develop the next generation. She later joined the Syrian Football Association (SFA), taking on administrative and coaching responsibilities.
A six-team women’s senior league was established in 2019, followed by the development of youth national teams. This year the country held an inaugural edition of its youth league. Al-Katreb developed Syria’s first women’s football strategy, submitted to Fifa, that set out a longer-term plan for expanding participation and creating a pathway into the national teams. “You have to start building from the bottom if you want to see results after these 10 years,” Al-Katreb said. “So that we don’t burn one generation after another.”
In 2022, women accounted for only 1,000 of Syria’s 25,000 registered footballers. The women’s football strategy, seen by the Guardian, aimed to increase female participation by 150% over four years, including through 33 school training centres across 11 provinces, with capacity for 1,650 girls by 2026.

items.title: Consistently inconsistent? Ten things we've learnt about Alonso's Chelsea so far
items.summary:
Chelsea: Ten things we've learnt about Xabi Alonso's Blues after 10 Premier League games
From a battle to be No 1 and various midfield combinations to set-pieces and systems, there's plenty to pick out from Xabi Alonso's start at Chelsea; Here we examine 10 takeaways so far; Follow Chelsea vs Leeds
items.text:
Chelsea: Ten things we've learnt about Xabi Alonso's Blues after 10 Premier League games
From a battle to be No 1 and various midfield combinations to set-pieces and systems, there's plenty to pick out from Xabi Alonso's start at Chelsea; Here we examine 10 takeaways so far; Follow Chelsea vs Leeds on Saturday with our live blog on the Sky Sports website and App, kick-off 3pm
Wednesday 18 November 2026 19:23, UK
Xabi Alonso's Chelsea project is 10 Premier League games in. Here's what we've learnt so far...
1 - Could Mike Penders become the preferred option to No 1 Emi Martinez?
Goalkeeper has been a long-standing problem position at Chelsea. Xabi Alonso spoke positively about his keeping options after taking charge but a night to forget for Robert Sanchez at Fulham in the Spaniard's first game in charge pushed the club into action. The 2022 World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez seemed like a no-brainer. However, the 34-year-old let three goals in on his debut against Brighton and hasn't looked totally assured.
An injury to the Argentine has created an opportunity for the highly rated Mike Penders. A calamitous own goal for the 21-year-old against Spurs was a terrible way to mark his first Premier League start but his response has been impressive. It is food for thought that Penders has a positive Expected Goals Against vs Actual Goals Conceded ratio (4.49 vs only three let in). Martinez's return is negative - 11 goals conceded from shots worth 9.17.
Petr Cech was just 22 when he made his Chelsea debut and went on to achieve legendary status. Alonso evidently didn't believe the Belgian international was ready at the start of this campaign but Penders has certainly given his manager something to consider.
2 - Inconsistent Chelsea's longest winning streak in the Premier League so far
Chelsea have been consistently inconsistent so far. They bounced back from a poor draw with Hull and even worse thumping at Brentford by dishing out a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth, while losses to Spurs and Sunderland have tempered expectations. Three games in, their trip to the Emirates was billed as an opportunity to show they could be a real threat - potentially even title contenders. Instead, after 10 games, they're 11 points behind Arsenal and unlikely to trouble the Premier League champions.
They've won back-to-back league games just twice and have yet to demonstrate evidence of a clear identity forming. Injuries to key personnel have hampered Alonso. The Chelsea boss has continually stated his side will look different in May, compared to what we are witnessing now. However, the journey and the eventual destination isn't obvious. Yet in spite of four league defeats already, the Blues are relatively well-placed for Champions League qualification.
3 - Games in a row without a recognised striker
We'll come onto Joao Pedro's brilliant start but Alonso's curious approach to his recent injury issue has sparked debate. Chelsea started without a recognised striker against Spurs, Man Utd and Sunderland, with Danny Welbeck given just a few minutes off the bench in the first two of those games before going on after an hour as Chelsea chased an equaliser at the Stadium of Light. With summer signings Welbeck and Emmanuel Emegha not trusted and Liam Delap, Nicolas Jackson and Marc Guiu sold, Chelsea look short up front.
Morgan Rogers and Pedro Neto have been used as false nines. The former Aston Villa man offers a presence when deployed there but Neto's usage is difficult to comprehend. Welbeck has been ineffective in starts against Brentford and Liverpool in the cup but Chelsea lack a focal point without a natural forward. They also have the biggest positive difference between goals scored (19) and Expected Goals (15.9). While that is the result of some stunning strikes, it also raises questions about the long-term sustainability of their attacking threat after blanks against Tottenham and Sunderland.
4 - Back four? Or back three?
In pre-season, there was much debate about whether Alonso would utilise the back-three set-up which served him so well at Bayer Leverkusen or go with a four as he did at Real Madrid. The answer is: a bit of both. There have been six matches when Chelsea have started with a four and four when they've gone with a three.
Alonso has been keen to stress that in-play shape is more significant than how the names are laid out in a graphic but his variations suggest he is still searching for the right formula - and Chelsea's inconsistent performances and results reflect that uncertainty. Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana have failed to convince at the start of this season and Maxence Lacroix is not injured. Academy graduate Josh Acheampong has been the only major positive defensively so far. He has mightily impressed.
5 - Times Chelsea have had more or less possession
Beyond formations, preconceptions about the style of play under Alonso have also been challenged in these opening 10 games. In half of them, Chelsea have had more possession than their opponents and bossed the ball. But it's been a different story in the other matches.
In fact, it was stunning to see Chelsea register just 26 per cent possession at home to Brighton in a game they won 4-3. They had just 31 per cent of the ball at home to Spurs. A performance which deeply frustrated the home support.
Part of the plan or a stat which speaks to deeper issues around controlling matches and winning midfield battles? Alonso has admitted that he wants his team to be better with the ball, a message he delivered at half-time to spark an upturn in performance against Manchester United.
6 - Different midfield combinations
Alonso was a midfield maestro in his playing days and he has made no secret of declaring the central area as key to his team's success. But he has tried six different midfield combinations so far.
