items.title: Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
items.summary:
Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
- Published
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitut
items.text:
Uganda deadly landslide survivors seek justice at the UN
- Published
Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
The landslide struck Bududa in 2019, killing more than 53 people, including 33 children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family members.
"My quest should be a lesson," he said.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.
"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.
The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.
"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change – and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
But the complainants say relocation must involve more than move people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported
items.text:
Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
- Published
Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, the AFP reported.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.

items.text:
The best European strikers this century - ranked by you
- Published
Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.
There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.
This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.
Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.
We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.
So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.
10. Karim Benzema
Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.
Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."
Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."
9. Ruud van Nistelrooy
Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.
The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.
Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."
Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."
8. Zlatan Ibrahimovic
Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.
Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."
Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."
Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."
7. Wayne Rooney
The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.
Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."
Balague: "What could have been, yes. He was the national team's record scorer too before Harry Kane took it. I find him to deserve this place as he had to adapt to a lot of strikers and he did it well. He had the ability to link up and score. He was very intelligent."
Laurens: "He is the most street footballer England has ever seen. There's no rules, that kind of anger you saw on the pitch. I don't think people in England realise how good he was."
6. Kylian Mbappe
What does becoming the all-time World Cup top goalscorer get you? Sixth place on the best European strikers this century list. The Real Madrid forward, 27, just misses out on the top five.
Laurens: "Maybe if we do this ranking again in a few years he will be higher. I would have had him top five, for sure. He has scored more than 400 goals. I don't think Messi and Ronaldo had scored that many at that age, so he's ahead. I don't know if he will play for as long as them but he hasn't done much wrong in his career."
Balague: "This list has to do what you feel about the player, not science - 22 goals in 22 appearances in World Cups and [Euro] Championships. He should be at least top three because of that. Great stats, but we're not in love with him."
Honigstein: "I don't think there is a forward that is as good as footballer as him in 2026. On that basis alone he should be higher, but people when they vote have other things in their head. The only way to win everyone over is to score more goals and win more World Cups for France, which I think is possible."
5. Erling Haaland
There was little between Mbappe and Erling Haaland, but it is Manchester City's prolific Norwegian who slips in at fifth. The 26-year-old has already scored more than 300 club goals and has a staggering 68 in 61 games for his country.
Balague: "Mbappe should be higher than him. Haaland scored 52 goals in 53 games [in 2022-23], that is astonishing, but he's gone 11 finals without scoring. We're talking about the best. We're talking about what we see at the moment and what we see is someone who is calculated but in a more charming way. An abilit

items.summary:
Anthony Joshua: British heavyweight boxer becomes dad for second time but unable to see daughter until after Tyson Fury fight
Anthony Joshua says ongoing training camp for his fight against Tyson Fury on December 11 means he will not see his new-born daughter until the days after the fight; "It's no
items.text:
Anthony Joshua: British heavyweight boxer becomes dad for second time but unable to see daughter until after Tyson Fury fight
Anthony Joshua says ongoing training camp for his fight against Tyson Fury on December 11 means he will not see his new-born daughter until the days after the fight; "It's not ideal but she is in good hands", says Joshua, who describes daughter's arrival as a "big blessing"
Thursday 19 November 2026 11:17, UK
Anthony Joshua became a father for the second time after the birth of a daughter last weekend, although ongoing training for his fight against Tyson Fury means he is not able to see her until mid-December.
Joshua, whose son JJ was born in 2015, is currently in training camp in Marbella in preparation for his blockbuster all-British fight against Fury on December 11 at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, and was unable to be at the birth.
Joshua says the arrival of his daughter, who has not yet been named, is "amazing" and "a big blessing" as the 37-year-old paid tribute to Nicole, the mother of both children.
- Opetaia withdraws from Wilder bout on Fury-AJ undercard
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📺
- Listen to the Toe2Toe podcast every week
While he has been able to have "many" FaceTime calls with mother and daughter in recent days, Joshua says he wished he would have been able to be there but preparations for the Fury fight mean mean he is currently "on a mission".
"It's not ideal but she is in good hands," Joshua said in an interview with The Sun.
"She's got an amazing mother, she's got amazing family round her and the people at the hospital, I heard they were amazing. I spoke to them and said thank you, so I'm pretty content at the minute that she's in good hands. But, for me, it would have been much better if I was able to be there.
"But I'm on duty at the minute and we're on a mission. I knew about this nine months ago so I made this commitment that I can't change, unfortunately, but there will be many more birthdays I'll be at, for sure."
Asked when he would likely meet her in person for the first time, Joshua said: "Probably December 12, December 13.
"I'll go and check in and rock her to sleep, let her hear my voice and let her feel my heartbeat, really. The basic stuff."
He said he would be a fully hands-on father.
"I'm going to do it all. I'm going to definitely do it all," he added.
"You might see me with some eye shadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse just trying to do the right thing by her."
Joshua said he had wanted to become a father for a second time to "do something positive" after the "painful and traumatic" experience of last December's car crash in Nigeria that killed two members of his team, personal trainer Latif Ayodele, and strength and conditioning coach Sina Ghami.
"After the year that I'm coming off I wanted to do something positive," said Joshua, who was injured in the crash.
"I wanted to give JJ the opportunity to be an older brother. One day I won't be here and he'll have a sibling that he can turn to, be with and plan their future together. It's nice to have a sibling that they can lean on each other when needed, when me and his mum aren't here one day in the future."
The British boxer added: "Nicole is doing good. She is healthy. She said it was an amazing experience. She said it was easier than JJ and she's much prettier than JJ, so she's happy! She's already deeply in love with her."

items.title: Maine Road offer non-league haven to fans of scandal-hit Manchester City
items.summary:
It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”
It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League
items.text:
It began with a timely message on social media. “We’ve seen the posts. We’ve read the comments. If all the recent conversation has made you curious about the other team in Manchester playing in sky blue, come and see us.”
It was a direct response to the news of a guilty verdict in the Premier League’s financial fair play case against Manchester City and it came from the 10th-tier (step six) club Maine Road, who carry City’s colours and a near-identical badge, as well as the name of City’s previous home.
Maine Road stadium was demolished in 2003-04 and replaced by houses but two miles away, in a corner of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, Maine Road FC are playing in front of about 100 people on a cool November Saturday. The high-stakes surroundings of the Premier League seem a fair distance away, but Maine Road – founded in 1955 in Rusholme as a Manchester City supporters’ club team – have never professed to be City.
“There is FC United and Manchester United, who are intrinsically linked in terms of why that club exists,” says Rob McKay, Maine Road women’s head coach, watching as a fan as the men’s side draw 0-0 with Halewood Apollo in the North West Counties League First Division North. “This is not a protest club. The links with City have ebbed and flowed over the years. It’s just that they were playing out of the Maine Road social club when it formed.”
The chair and director Alex Simmonds, who arrived in the summer, has big ambitions for Maine Road. He believes the fallout from City’s legal battle with the Premier League could help attract a new audience.
“It was a bit of a statement,” Simmonds says of that social media post. “We came across a lot of comments when the news came out and a lot were saying: ‘Well, we’ll stop watching City if they get relegated or if anything happens, and we’ll just go to Maine Road.’ That came up in quite a few conversations online.”
Simmonds admits there has not yet been a huge rise in crowd numbers, with City fans, perhaps understandably, staying defiantly loyal to their club, who have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict. His priority is to regenerate Maine Road. “For me coming into the club, it was about trying to get people to see that we are here,” he says. “To get in touch with the community and to get fans down here, so no matter who you support in the Premier League or Championship or whatever, we are here.”
Maine Road offer free entry to anyone with a season ticket for a Premier League or EFL club, hoping to boost numbers during international breaks or when other Greater Manchester teams play away. Simmonds is helping to fund a multimillion-pound renovation of St Margaret’s Community Centre, which serves as Maine Road’s clubhouse. The club are also launching a new website and a scheme to hand out thousands of free tickets to local primary schools.
Will that, combined with potential disillusionment after any City punishment, bring fans flocking to Maine Road? “I think it will,” Simmonds says, “but only if people know that there’s a difference between a Premier League Man City and a Maine Road at step six. If they come with ideas that we are going to be a City or even one of the bigger semi-pro teams … we’re not quite there yet. But their support would help.”
Non-league football in Greater Manchester has enjoyed a significant surge in popularity since Covid, so Maine Road find themselves in a crowded marketplace. McKay says: “West Didsbury and Chorlton are down the road and they get 1,000. Droylsden get huge crowds, Ashton United get huge crowds, Curzon Ashton are getting reasonable crowds. There’s so much football.”
Simmonds believes the connection with City, however loose, should help Maine Road gradually gain a foothold. City’s former training ground at Platt Lane is a stone’s throw from Brantingham Road, where Maine Road play. City’s academy teams have played at Maine Road’s ground, as well as at nearby St Bede’s College.
Another connection is the fact Maine Road are managed by a former City player in Leon Mike, who made his only City start at the old Maine Road in 2001 under Kevin Keegan.
“People make jokes about the Etihad not being full, but genuinely, a lot of times you speak to City fans, they’ll say it’s too expensive,” says Mike. “Premier League, FA Cup, League Cup, Champions League, that’s a lot of games to go to. Whereas on a Saturday here it will cost you £6 to attend and you can have a pint and some food.”
There is optimism among those most closely connected with Maine Road that the club will soon experience growth. “We gained 9,000 followers across the platforms just on the back of that one social media post,” Simmonds says. “It was surprising – I didn’t think it would do that – but social media is really powerful. We’re definitely going to try and stay in that conversation and get people coming through.”

The Premier League is back after the recent international break and the Sky Sports football writers dissect all the major talking points ahead of another busy weekend's action.
Man City vs Fulham: Cottagers ideal opponents to get City back to winning ways
Are Man City in crisis heading into Saturday lunchtime's clash against Fulham, with Enzo Maresca's side having lost their previous three Premier League contests to lose top spot to Arsenal?
Those trio of reverses against Aston Villa, Brighton and, just prior to the international break, Nottingham Forest, mean City have now lost as many times as in their previous 36 league outings.
Since the start of 2007-08, though, City have only been beaten in four successive top-flight games on two occasions, in August 2008 and December 2024, and it would take a massive leap of faith to suggest Fulham are the team to inflict such ignominy on them this weekend.
In fact, if Maresca could pick one side to face to get back to winning ways, it would be Fulham, who City have got the better of in each of their last 17 Premier League encounters, scoring at least twice each time.
Rich Morgan

Aston Villa vs Sunderland: Can Villa recover after sour note or will Black Cats begin to build?
Aston Villa left for the international break on a sour note after squandering a two-goal lead on two occasions at Old Trafford for their dramatic 4-4 draw against Manchester United.
Sunderland, meanwhile, secured a much-needed 1-0 win against Chelsea to relieve the pressure on Regis Le Bris.
His side remain in the bottom three because of their poor start to the season and a win at Villa Park is a big ask, especially given injuries to Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey, but it will be needed if talks of his departure are going to fizzle out.
The Black Cats have not travelled well this term with just one win on the road, which came in their narrow escape at Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, but Villa Park's crackling atmosphere has been dampened by the closure of the North Stand this season.
Injuries, storylines and ramifications. Plus, if it is anything like their last meeting at Villa Park, a dramatic 4-3 win for Villa courtesy of Tammy Abraham's injury-time winner, then this is one you will be wanting to follow along in the Sky Sports live blog.
Pat Rowe
Coventry vs Palace: Manager bounce or manager bump? Eagles might be in for a nasty surprise
The managerial merry-go-round is spinning again. Crystal Palace have jumped aboard, handing Thomas Frank the keys to Selhurst Park. New hope. But a new manager doesn't necessarily mean new results.
In fact, recent evidence suggests quite the opposite for teams in trouble.
The famous 'new manager bounce' is one of football's most romanticised theories. A fresh face walks through the door, standards supposedly rise overnight and points start rolling in.
Shame the numbers don't back it up.
Of the last six Premier League teams sitting in the bottom eight to change manager between November and March, five actually saw their points-per-game average drop across the following five matches.
Vitor Pereira at Nottingham Forest. Igor Tudor at Tottenham. Rob Edwards at Wolves. Graham Potter at West Ham. Ivan Juric at Southampton.
It's a fascinating trend that should serve as a warning to Palace supporters expecting Frank to arrive waving a magic wand.
The reality is that struggling teams usually have deep-rooted problems that can't be solved by a few tactical tweaks and an inspirational team talk. Confidence, structure and, ultimately, quality of players tend to outweigh a difference voice in the dugout.
Coventry are next up for Palace and Frank will be desperate to buck the trend.
But history suggests the bounce might be more of a bump.
Lewis Jones
Bournemouth vs Forest: Can Cherries pick up one more win to make club history?
Bournemouth couldn't buy a Premier League victory in the opening six weeks or so of the season, but over the last month they have looked like an unstoppable force. Now they can't stop winning.
Since a 3-0 win over Sturm Graz in the Europa League on October 15, the Cherries have won four in a row in the Premier League, three in a row in Europe and once in the Carabao Cup, booking a spot in the quarter-finals.
Eight wins in succession in all competitions; a club record equalled.
It's made even more astonishing when you realise Marco Rose has only been in charge for 16 games. And that it's the club's first ever season in Europe. And that those eight wins came within a period of just 25 days.
With the schedule that lies ahead, the run will naturally come under threat sooner rather than later, but where's the harm in trying to squeeze out one more win to make history?
Dan Long
Tottenham vs Ipswich: Stop Enciso, stop Tractor Boys?
Ipswich have a Julio Enciso problem. Not because the Paraguayan isn't delivering the goods. Quite the opposite. He's become so influential to their attacking output that stopping him is the key to stopping Ipswich.
Bournemouth certainly cracked it before the international break.
Their 2-1 victory over Ipswich was a tactical lesson in how to suffocate a team reliant on one creative spark. Cut off the supply lines into Enciso, deny him the space to weave his magic and ask the rest of the Ipswich attack to come up with the answers.
The numbers were quite staggering. Despite trailing for almost the entire game, Ipswich created just 0.30 worth of expected go

Max Verstappen says he trusts F1 bosses over plans to proceed with season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid conflict in Middle East
Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubt
items.text:
Max Verstappen says he trusts F1 bosses over plans to proceed with season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid conflict in Middle East
Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubts; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Thursday 19 November 2026 08:21, UK
Max Verstappen says he trusts Formula 1 to "make the right call" as the sport pushes on with plans to hold the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi despite continued conflict in the Middle East.
F1 had to cancel races scheduled in April in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, but the Qatar Grand Prix from November 27-29 and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 4-6 are currently set to go ahead.
While F1 bosses had maintained throughout the year that their intention was to proceed with the events as planned, it was only after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on November 8 that a contingency plan to hold a season-ending race in Italy was aborted.

Therefore, Wednesday evening's media sessions ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, which forms a season-ending triple header with the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, was the first opportunity for the drivers to publicly react to the latest developments.
Red Bull's Verstappen, who had in September voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East, appears to have changed his position.
The four-time world champion said on Wednesday: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?
"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.
"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."
While there haven't been notable recent incidents in Qatar or Abu Dhabi, a US military base in Bahrain was targeted over the weekend, and Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the country's Saudi Arabian backed government.
Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc acknowledged that the situation remains "tricky" but also expressed faith that F1 and the sport's governing body, the FIA, will act responsibly.
"It's a situation that is kind of tricky," Leclerc said. "At the same, I feel like we are up to date with whatever is organised, and I guess that on our side we have to trust the process, and that's what I'll do.
"I'm sure the FIA is taking everything seriously to make sure that everybody is safe. It's in the best interest of absolutely everyone.
"So, yeah, me as a driver, I'll just trust that process, and be in Qatar if it's safe to be there."
Norris, Russell reassured by friends in region
British drivers Lando Norris and George Russell both said they have been reassured by friends of theirs who live in the Middle East.
Russell often represents his rivals in his role as a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GPDA), but he explained that the seriousness of the situation has resulted in that organisation having little involvement.
"We're [the GPDA] not involved because it's way above our heads, and the truth is, we will be going if nothing is escalated," the Mercedes driver said.
"F1 is not making those decisions, it's the people in the high powers of politics.
"I trust in Formula 1. I'm not concerned. I know a lot of people who live in the region, and they say pretty bluntly, 'we're living there with our families, and if we didn't feel safe, we wouldn't be.'
"They feel safe as it is, and I'm sure and I hope everything will be ok."
Norris revealed that he will be attending a friend's wedding in Bahrain ahead of the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but said he was more concerned for members of his McLaren team than himself.
"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," the 2025 world champion said.
"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

items.text:
How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
And the gap is growing. Every season.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Big six get richer and the gap grows
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
Let's look at how the gap has grown.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
So what has driven this huge escalation?
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.
"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
Champions League widens the gulf
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Stamford Bridge - Chelsea's big problem
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and City.
Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.
"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
How new rules allow big six to spend even more
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

items.text:
From Forest fringes to Glasner's go-to guy - the rise of McAtee
- Published
"James McAtee is probably one of the winners of this pre-season."
Oliver Glasner's immediate impression of his Nottingham Forest midfielder foretold the faith the head coach has shown in him.
Forest appear to have found their Elliot Anderson replacement from within as McAtee has become a key man for the Austrian.
After his £30m move from Manchester City in 2025, McAtee endured a difficult start to life at the City Ground.
Yet he played a key role as Forest toppled City and the returning Anderson before the international break for their first home win of the season.
There has been no clamour for an England call, but has Thomas Tuchel unfairly overlooked McAtee - and how has he gone from the Forest bench to indispensable?
The City academy graduate made only two Premier League starts last season, one of the bigger victims of Forest's revolving door as the club went through four managers.
Nine starts in Forest's run to the Europa League semi-finals could not hide a campaign of frustration.
It was supposed to be a platform after captaining England Under-21s to Euro 2025 victory, but he played only 289 minutes in the league.
The 24-year-old has already tripled those minutes this season after becoming a key player for Glasner, starting every top-flight game.
It followed the manager suggesting in the summer that McAtee could replace Anderson following his £116m move to City - something which left McAtee unsure.
"When I first came in and [Glasner] put me in the [number] six [role] on the second day in my head I was like: 'oh, he's not seeing me in his plans, I'm playing deeper'," he said at Forest's training ground.
"My confidence is growing, but not fully there yet, but I think we're on our way.
"I thought I had it in my locker, but I never thought he would actually try it out with me in pre-season.
"I think Ibra [Sangare] was injured at the time so I was thinking, I'm just going in for Ibra. But then as pre-season got on and I was playing there I felt more comfortable."
It was evidence of McAtee's work after he worked throughout the summer to return for pre-season.
He trained with former Plymouth, Leeds and Ipswich midfielder David Norris, now a personal trainer, and put on 2.5kg of muscle while losing 1kg of fat.
Weight sessions followed fitness work in the morning, which is what prompted Glasner to credit his summer of work.
The relationship with Glasner has been crucial. The Forest boss has offered clarity and calmness to a squad which endured the chaos last season.
A post-match inquest following the 2-0 defeat by Brentford sparked the right response from the squad, after a start which has left them 16th in the league.
After McAtee failed to find consistency and rhythm last season, Glasner promised him he would be afforded time and the benefit of the doubt if he had a poor game.
"I think [last season] was a me problem. I was struggling to get my chance," he said, having used a psychologist before the start of pre-season.
"I've never really had a season like that, I was always in and out. It was frustrating, but as frustrating as it was, it was a good lesson.
"As I saw my confidence kept going worse and worse and worse. As I've watched clips of me, I can tell when I was going a little bit under.
"This year, if I make a pass and I lose it, it won't bother me as much because I've been through that."
McAtee has always had supporters at the City Ground. All four managers were impressed by his training levels last season, but he was always under pressure to deliver when given a brief chance.
Forest technical director George Syrianos has also championed the calls internally for McAtee.
It has allowed McAtee - whose brother John plays for Bolton - to feel the faith, having learned from previous difficulties, with England on his mind.
He is eager to make the step up to Tuchel's senior side, and has supporters at the Football Association.
He prioritised playing for the U21s at Euro 2025 - captaining them to victory - over going to the Club World Cup with City, and underlined his determination to represent his country to manager Pep Guardiola and director of football Txiki Begiristain at the time.
Now, under Glasner, after a difficult first season, McAtee has that platform with Euro 2028 a realistic target.
"At this moment I need to have a good year for me to maybe be in with the chance of getting picked, but the competition in the position I'm playing is so high," he said.
"If I could add some goals, some stats, it could put me within a chance to be around that circle. The competition is very elite at the moment, but that's the aim, that's the goal."
Against City, he was moved further forward, with Ryan Yates coming in to add more bodies in midfield.
But the stats back up McAtee's improvement and he compares favourably to others.
He has made the most final-third passes for Forest (151) and has played the joint-most through balls with Morgan Gibbs-White (five). His 426 passes are behind only Murillo's 501, and he has created 18 chances - six short of Gibbs-White.
McAtee is only 29m behind Gibbs-White, having carried the ball 1,180m this season, but has made the most carries with 109 and has won possession back 63 times - winning 53% of his ground duels, indicating he has developed more of a mean streak in his game.
He has comfortably outperformed Everton's James Garner - one of his rivals for a place in the England squad - creating more chances, making more forward passes, winning more defensive duels and making more successful tackles.
McAtee has also made more recoveries, successful tackles, passes and clearances than Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton.
Now, having gone under the radar this season, come the next international break in March, Tuchel may not be able to ignore him.

items.title: Bancroft speaks again after explosive Sandpapergate claims
items.summary:
Cameron Bancroft: Former Australia batter says he feels 'very free' after 'telling the truth' with Sandpapergate claims
Cameron Bancroft says he "never meant to point fingers or implicate others; "I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth;" in making his statement on the 2018 ball tamper
items.text:
Cameron Bancroft: Former Australia batter says he feels 'very free' after 'telling the truth' with Sandpapergate claims
Cameron Bancroft says he "never meant to point fingers or implicate others; "I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth;" in making his statement on the 2018 ball tampering scandal; meanwhile, Pat Cummins' manager says Test captain has been "consistent and adamant from day one"
Thursday 19 November 2026 07:58, UK
Cameron Bancroft says he feels "very free" following his explosive claims about the Sandpapergate scandal.
In a 4,000-word statement in The West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, Bancroft broke his silence on revelations in Usman Khawaja's new book, claiming that Cummins' press conference denying the allegations was the "final straw" for him, revealing that the entire bowling unit maintained full knowledge of the extensive use of sandpaper.
Bancroft saw his career turned upside after being suspended for his part in the 2018 incident alongside then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner. Those were the only three players to be punished.
Speaking to local media on Thursday, Bancroft said: "I never meant to point fingers or implicate others; I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth.
"This has been a burden that I've carried with me for such a long period of time but I feel very free and I feel very happy that I've been able to do that."
Footage on social media on Thursday also showed Cummins being approached for comment by local TV reporters when leaving his house for training with New South Wales. The Australian Test captain declined to address Bancroft's remarks.
A statement from his manager, Neil Maxwell, said: "Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one.
"Pat feels for Cam [Bancroft] of course. He has been through a lot. We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said."
Bancroft's statement has heaped pressure on Test captain Cummins, with Australia's next red-ball series against New Zealand beginning on December 9.
The claims come in the wake of a furore of discussion around the 2018 scandal, with Khawaja's book first bringing to light claims that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper.
Khawaja also alleged that discussions about ball-tampering had been held "openly and lightheartedly" across the entire squad, involving not just the batters, bowlers and coaching staff but the wider team.
Cummins dismissed Khawaja's claims as "complete and utter nonsense" during a sensational 68-minute press conference last Friday.
Bancroft's statement came just after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum to explore the scandal, stating that players could share their version of events without fears of reprisals - a decision which Khawaja and David Warner have questioned.

items.text:
Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.
Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kylian Mbappe
Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.
The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.
Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.
It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.
Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.
He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.
Rodri
Age: 30 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield
Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.
By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.
His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.
His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.
Lamine Yamal
Age: 19 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

items.text:
Formula 1 drivers back return of 'very cool' V8 engines in the future ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix
Several Formula 1 drivers have backed the possibility of V8 engines returning to the sport as early as 2030; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 06:47, UK
Formula 1's drivers appear to be unanimous with the prospect of V8 engine returning to the sport in the 2030s.
Earlier this week, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem teased the possibility of V8 engines with the sound of a screaming F1 car with a caption: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."
The FIA also published graphics on social media which suggested an agreement in principle had been reached by themselves, Formula 1 management and the engine manufacturers for V8 engines to return from 2030, but the post was deleted.
- Las Vegas GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
The current regulations are set to run until 2031, which could be an explanation for the deleted post, while further details of the overall power unit, including whether an electrical element and a turbo will remain, need to be finalised.
"I'd love to see it. When I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps," said Mercedes driver George Russell.
"I think it's about just that high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era. The purists will say take away all electrical power, but I think when you look at how a lot of these cars have evolved in recent years, and the power output from some of these electrical motors these days, Formula 1 is going to continue to be the fastest race cars on the planet, you need to have it, that's just the reality.
"You need to have some sort of hybrid, because the power you get, you can't really produce that just solely on internal combustion.
"If we go back to V8s, having some sort of electrical power as well, to give you that extra 400, 500 kilowatts to bring the cars to 1000+ horsepower, that's what we want.
"I think it's worth remembering as well actually, the final V8 era, they sounded awesome, but the cars, they actually weren't very fast. I don't think many people realise that."
New world champion Kimi Antonelli agreed with his Mercedes team-mate and claims "many people would look forward" to the return of V8 engines.
"It's going be very cool to go back to more old style. Also, the cars will get lighter even further, probably 70kg, which is immense," he said.
"Definitely, I think it's a very exciting regulation change. Of course, we have got to first do well in this one."
Verstappen: F1 going in the right direction
Max Verstappen has been critical of the current power units which are around 53 per cent battery powered and led to an unusual style of driving and racing at some tracks, with the drivers sometimes unable to push flat out in a traditional manner.
Verstappen, who warned driving in Las Vegas will be "painful" due to the long straights, feels the FIA have listened to the drivers and realised the 2026 regulations are "not what you want".
The four-time world champion stated he would get rid of the turbo in future power unit regulations, and effectively have a fully normally aspirated engine.
"In some tracks then you're not allowed to race because it will be too loud because if it's up to me I would take the turbo off," he explained.
"I would get rid, maybe you can use it as a push to pass, but not too much of the battery side. But then on some tracks, you're not allowed to race, so fuel consumption goes up a lot without a turbo, so you need a bigger tank if you don't want to do refuelling in the races, so I understand that you want to have a turbo.
"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that not something realistic.
"This [news] is good. This is for sure in the right direction, but again, it's not confirmed yet. So there's still a few things I guess that they need to agree on."
Lewis Hamilton, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are the only drivers who drove in the previous V8 era which ended in 2013.
Alonso said it's "frustrating" F1 has not had V8 engines since 2014, while Hamilton is keen to know more details about the proposed return of V8s.
"I think it's ultimately dependent on… it's all well going to V8. It depends on how they design it, regulation-wise, and going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era," he said.
"Yeah, bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.
"But you could have that, and as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that'd be better."

items.summary:
Lauren Price hopes making undisputed history could lead her to Claressa Shields showdown: 'I want the big fights'
Olympic gold medallist Lauren Price wants to test herself against Claressa Shields, Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer; Price will become Wales' first undisputed world champion in the f
items.text:
Lauren Price hopes making undisputed history could lead her to Claressa Shields showdown: 'I want the big fights'
Olympic gold medallist Lauren Price wants to test herself against Claressa Shields, Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer; Price will become Wales' first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era if she beats Michaela Kotaskova and hopes victory can lead to American star Shields
Wednesday 18 November 2026 18:02, UK
Lauren Price believes becoming an undisputed champion could lead her to a showdown with American star Claressa Shields.
Price faced off with Shields after her last fight but no agreement has been reached for them to box.
Shields has been an undisputed champion in multiple divisions and has returned to middleweight after a period as the undisputed heavyweight champion.
Price, like Shields, won the Olympic gold medal at middleweight. She's unbeaten as a professional too. On Friday Price looks to add the now vacant WBO welterweight title to the WBA, WBC and IBF belts she already holds when she fights Michaela Kotaskova.
If she wins she will become Wales' first undisputed champion in the four-belt era.
"It hasn't sunk in yet," Price told Sky Sports. "When I turned over, that's the dream to become undisputed. I can honestly say if I achieve that on Friday then I've ticked every accolade in boxing.
"Regardless of the belts on the line, you step through the ropes and it's another fight. I just let the boxing do the talking and make sure I get that win and I win in style."
If Price does go undisputed at welterweight, moving up through divisions will be the natural next step. Shields remains a target though that fight is yet to come to fruition.
"It has to make sense on both ends," Price said. "I'm giving away weight, fine. But it was in her back garden, I wanted to come back to Wales as well.
"I believe it will happen."
On December 24 Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer, who vacated the WBO welterweight title, will rematch for the WBA, WBC and WBO super-welter championships. Price has an eye on fighting the winner.
"They're both great. But I believe Chantelle will win that fight again and that's a great fight for British boxing, I'm 100 percent up for it," Price said.
"I think right now obviously myself, Cameron, Mayer's in there [the pound-for-pound list] and obviously Shields. For me we're the big names and that's what I want, I want the big fights."

items.title: Hamilton denies lack of trust with Ferrari after strategy issues
items.summary:
Lewis Hamilton denies lack of trust with Ferrari after ignoring instructions from pit wall twice in recent races
Lewis Hamilton ignored instructions from his Ferrari team to pit at recent races in Singapore and Brazil; the Brit insists there is no trust issue; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky S
items.text:
Lewis Hamilton denies lack of trust with Ferrari after ignoring instructions from pit wall twice in recent races
Lewis Hamilton ignored instructions from his Ferrari team to pit at recent races in Singapore and Brazil; the Brit insists there is no trust issue; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Thursday 19 November 2026 06:13, UK
Lewis Hamilton has insisted there is no lack of trust between himself and his Ferrari team despite having overridden orders from the pit wall twice in recent races.
At the Singapore Grand Prix in October and the Sao Paulo Grand Prix earlier this month, Hamilton ignored instructions to pit, with his decision costing him places on both occasions.
The incidents followed several moments earlier in the season where Hamilton had been left frustrated by strategic decisions from Ferrari that failed to optimise his chances.
- Las Vegas GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Asked ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix whether taking matters into his own hands was indicative of a lack of trust, Hamilton insisted he was pleased with the work of his race engineer Carlo Santi.
The seven-time world champion said: "No, it's definitely not trusting. I think it's just we're constantly working on our communication. I think that it's been a lot better this year.
"Carlo has done an amazing job, and I think there's been a couple of times where it's just those particular two times was not, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed, and I got the call at the last minute.
"And we'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united and working, I think in the right direction."
'No concerns about racing Leclerc'
Hamilton has also had to handle controversy with his team-mate Charles Leclerc, after a first-lap clash between the pair at the Mexico City Grand Prix resulted in something of a public fall out.
Hamilton was highly critical of Leclerc for aggressively attempting to challenge him for the lead on the first lap, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen taking advantage of the squabble to win a race that Ferrari likely would have claimed a one-two in had their drivers held position.
Both Hamilton and Leclerc said that a conversation in Brazil the week after the incident had resolved the situation, and the Brit on Wednesday reiterated his confidence in their working relationship moving forwards.
"I think Charles is a great driver," Hamilton said. "I think, as I said, the detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.
"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.
"So, I don't feel that that will be a problem moving forwards, and I have no concerns or worries about racing him. I don't think he does with me either."
Can Ferrari challenge in Las Vegas?
Hamilton admitted he is unsure whether Ferrari will be able to challenge for victory in Las Vegas given the circuit is unlikely to suit their car.
The circuit's long straight could expose Ferrari's power unit weaknesses, while the cold temperatures could lead to issues heating up their tyres sufficiently.
Hamilton said: "We've had a car that's been quick through corners. Obviously, yeah, you have the long straight here. I don't know how that's going to be for us.
"We'll do the best job we can, but hopefully we can make up some of the time maybe in some of the corners. We'll have to wait and see."
Regardless of how competitive Ferrari are, Hamilton says the team will use this weekend, and the upcoming final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, to attempt to optimise their plans for the start of the 2027 season.
"This is a period of time… we don't have any new components to test, but this is definitely a really important data point for us to understand and make some changes setup wise, and try some things that we can potentially try to see if everything's working, if there's different elements of the car that we can remove or add, thinking about next year," he said.
"There's some big changes for next year. But otherwise, right now we have to focus on maintain second in the constructors' championship."

items.title: 15M web servers on one VM – smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
items.summary:
15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them
items.text:
15 million web servers on one VM - smoltcp, DPDK, AF_XDP
Put a web server online and everyone starts trying to hack it. Why? A basic rule of economics. Short supply, big demand - there aren’t enough web servers for everyone. Let’s run a web server for every human on the planet, all 8 billion of them. I couldn’t get funding, so we’re bootstrapping. The goal is to run 15 million web servers on one VM with 10GB of RAM and 1 CPU core. If we succeed, I’ll find some RAM from old microwaves around the house and we’ll scale it up so everyone can have their own web server. Demand will drop to zero and cybersecurity will be solved once and for all.
Web server
Instead of vibe coding it all, let’s use an ancient technique called learning. First of all, what is a web server? There are a few essential syscalls.
- listen - syscall, asks kernel to listen for connections on a socket
- accept - syscall, accepts a connection on a socket
- recv - receives data from a socket
- send - sends data
- close - closes
What is a syscall? A function that is executed by the OS kernel. Whatever fancy language or library you use for HTTP, it all comes down to those syscalls (well, yes, but actually no). Let’s use C to make it all explicit. We start listening, then read from the socket in a loop and always reply with OK.
int main(void)
{
    // We use port 0 which makes OS return any available port
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0); 
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}
It couldn’t be simpler: listen on a socket, accept a connection, read the data, send a reply, close the client connection, and repeat. It gives us around 65k RPS. Now that we’ve learned everything, let’s finish the article and call it a day:
$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server &; done
...
...
28232
program exited with error 1
Hm, why did listen fail? Ah, we’ve run out of ports! We’re using port=0, so the kernel picks an available port from ip_local_port_range.
$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768    60999
Why are so many ports skipped? Historically, port 0 was created for outbound connections. When you call connect('example.com', 80), Linux connects to the remote server (the sending part) and then allocates a random port on the host from ip_local_port_range to receive data (the receiving part). There are a few reasons the default range is small.
- Port 0 is special. You cannot listen on it (actually, you can - https://acid.vegas/blog/the-port-that-does-not-exist/).
- Ports 1-1024 require root.
- Ports 1024-32768 are skipped to keep dynamically allocated ports from conflicting with existing apps. You don’t want to call connect('example.com') and end up allocating port 3306 to receive incoming data. mysql cannot start because you have example.com open in your Firefox would make for a confusing UX.
- Ports 60999 - 65535 are excluded for historical reasons dating back to IP Masquerading.
Nothing prevents us from overriding the range and using 1-65535, but that’s still a bit short of 15 million. A UDP server and a TCP server can use the same port, so we can double that to 128k. We could run a proxy in front to forward requests to the right process (virtual hosting, yay), but these are all ancient techniques - in the AI era, whenever you have a software problem, you just throw money at the hardware. Let’s simply connect 15M/32k=450 new network cards to the server.
The 65k limit comes from the TCP standard. A port is a u16, so even if we hack the kernel with find '*.c' -exec sed -i 's/u16/u32/' \; to support bigger port numbers, normal clients still wouldn’t be able to connect. Each listening server is identified by a (protocol, IP, port) tuple. That explains how we can use the same port for UDP and TCP. It also means we can use a bunch of different IPs for our web servers. If we connect 450 network cards to the server, we’ll get 450 unique IP addresses and be able to listen on 15 million unique addresses!
UPD. I’ve heard from readers that the network card is the ONLY hardware component that didn’t get 100 times more expensive in the last year. Can’t we avoid ruining that too and solve this in software?
Let’s use a beautiful technology called AnyIP, which lets us listen on a whole subnet. Many VPS and dedicated server providers routinely give you a whole TCPv6 subnet. We can simply run sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo to get 18 quintillion addresses (plus or minus one) to listen on. You can do the same for IPv4 - acquiring a subnet with 15M addresses would cost around $250 million, so adjust the command for your environment. We’ll change our server to pick the nth IP from our range:
// Read IP index from CLI, shift base IP by it
int i = read_cli_param(argv[1]);
const uint32_t base_ip = 0x0a400001;  // ex. 10.64.0.1
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(first_ip + i);  // shift, ex. 10.64.0.2
And now we can finally finish the article.
$ for i in $(seq 1 15_000_000); do echo $i; ./server $i &; done
...
...
Out of memory
Hm, one server consumes 1.5MB of RAM, so running that many would take… 20TB of RAM, which is a few bytes more than our 10GB budget.
Runtime
By pure coincidence (what are the odds?), I explained in Running 10 million Codex CLIs on one server - LFI processes why running millions of processes creates too much overhead. The answer is to run them all in one process inside a custom runtime, much as V8 can run millions of guests in a single process. In Userland Linux scheduler in Rust, I showed how to build a specialised userland scheduler and switch between tasks with the absolute minimum amount of RAM per task.
TLDR: We’re using LFI for sandboxing. It gives us memory i

items.text:
ruby2ßhell
A one-byte heap overflow to remote code execution in Ruby's string case conversion. Reachable without authentication in the default configuration of common Ruby web frameworks and self-hosted software.
- Severity
- Critical
- Fixed in
- 3.3.14, 3.4.13, 4.0.10
- Access needed
- Network, no authentication
- Advisory
- GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 CVE pending
Affected software
Ruby versions
Your deployment
The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.
Self-hosted software
The latest version of the following popular software bundles an affected Ruby.
Updated .
Remediation
Your deployment
Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.
Self-hosted software
Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.
Technical details
Root cause
Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital
ß. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but
              the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).
The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20
              bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an
              input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.
The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings
              and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by
upcase, swapcase,
downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.
UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.
Fixed upstream in
ruby/ruby@d582f8f.
Primitive
A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S
(0x53) when upcasing or s
(0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly
              after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the
              buffer through the input length.
Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.
Proof of concept
We'll be publishing a proof of concept in a week, once people have had time to upgrade.

items.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
items.summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying
items.text:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.
The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.
“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.
For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”
He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”
He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”
But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”
When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.”
He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.”
In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.
